wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e111.summary: Poses the second principal incidental question: whether every property is demonstrable a priori of its first subject. It opens with the argument that some property is demonstrable and there is no reason why one should be rather than another, so all are.
claims: Some property is demonstrable (argument).

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e127.summary: Argument to the contrary: it was said earlier that 'creative' and similar terms cannot be demonstrated of God.
claims: 'Creative' cannot be demonstrated of God.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e134.summary: Distinguishes kinds of properties: (1) those importing absolute things really distinct from and formally inhering in their subjects ('susceptible of learning', 'heatable'); (2) those importing motion or change ('risible', 'mobile', 'alterable'); (3) connotative ones, which connote something extrinsic ('creative', 'calefactive'); (4) negative or privative ones.
claims: Properties divide into absolute-inherent, motion-importing, connotative, and negative or privative kinds.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e154.summary: First conclusion: no property importing an absolute thing that formally inheres is demonstrable of its first subject. The first subject is defined as that to which the property can belong with everything else set aside and to which nothing else can when it is set aside. The intellective soul is the first subject of 'susceptible of learning', while man is only a secondary subject, since the soul could still receive learning if the man were destroyed. The same holds for accidents that belong to a whole through a part.
claims: No property importing a formally inhering absolute thing is demonstrable of its first subject.
The first subject is that to which a property can belong with everything else removed and without which nothing has it.
The intellective soul, not man, is the first subject of susceptibility to learning.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e186.summary: First proof of the first conclusion: an immediate proposition cannot be demonstrated, and such a proposition is immediate.
claims: An immediate proposition cannot be demonstrated.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e202.summary: Objection: a proposition immediate by immediacy of subject, but not by immediacy of cause, can be demonstrated, as 'every triangle has three angles equal to two right angles' is.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e213.summary: Rejects the objection: per Aristotle an immediate proposition has none prior to it, so it cannot be demonstrated a priori. 'Subject' is ambiguous. It can mean one term of which something is predicable, and in this sense a proposition immediate in subject can be demonstrable (the triangle). Or it can mean everything of which something is predicable, and then not, since whatever is demonstrated belongs first to the middle term, which is then subject as well as cause. So the definition of the triangle, if it is the middle, is in one way the first subject of the property and the triangle in another.
claims: An immediate proposition has no prior proposition and cannot be demonstrated a priori.
'Subject' can mean one term or everything of which a predicate is said.
The middle term of a demonstration is itself a subject of the property.
The definition of triangle is in one sense the first subject of the angle-sum property.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e250.summary: An alternative reply that also yields a second proof. A proposition immediate in subject is demonstrable only through a definition that expresses parts determinate in number (the triangle's three lines) or in essence (matter and form for 'corruptible'). Each part is a cause of the property's inherence, since without any part the property would not belong. A property importing an inhering absolute thing has no such definition. Parts of the same kind cannot be determinate in number, because the property remains when any part is removed (a remainder is still heatable). Parts of different kinds are excluded because the first subject of an absolute accident is as simple as the accident.
claims: Propositions immediate in subject are demonstrable only through definitions expressing determinate parts.
Absolute inhering properties remain when any part of the subject is removed.
The first subject of an absolute accident is as simple as the accident.
So properties importing absolute inherent things cannot be demonstrated through definitions.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e320.summary: Third proof: a proposition whose first knowledge can only be had through experience, by means of some contingent proposition, is not demonstrable, and every such property-proposition is of this kind. The major holds because knowledge of the premises suffices for a demonstrable conclusion. The minor holds by induction: however much abstractive knowledge one has of the soul and of learning, the universal 'every intellective soul can receive learning' is never evident unless some singular such as 'this soul has learning' is known intuitively. If it were known from the terms it would be a principle, not a conclusion. Likewise 'fire can be hot' is known only by experience.
claims: What can first be known only through experience via a contingent proposition is not demonstrable.
Universal propositions about absolute properties become evident only through intuitive knowledge of singular instances.
A proposition known from its terms is a principle, not a conclusion.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e381.summary: Second conclusion: such a property can be demonstrated of a subject that is not its first subject.
claims: An absolute inhering property can be demonstrated of a non-first subject.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e389.summary: Distinguishes senses of 'non-first subject'. (1) Not coextensive in predication, either exceeding the first subject (figure relative to triangle) or exceeded by it (isosceles relative to triangle). (2) A whole relative to the first subject, as man relative to the intellective soul. (3) A substrate sustaining the first subject, as fire sustains heat. In the first case the property is demonstrated of a broader subject in a particular conclusion through the lower term ('some figure has three angles'), and of a narrower subject through the first subject. In the second and third cases it is demonstrated through the first subject as middle term ('whatever has an intellective soul is susceptible of learning; every man has one').
claims: A non-first subject may exceed, be exceeded by, be a whole of, or sustain the first subject.
Demonstration of a property of a broader subject is particular.
Demonstration of a property of a whole or substrate proceeds through the first subject as middle.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e454.summary: Third conclusion: among connotative properties that do not require a determinate distinction of parts, some are demonstrable and some are not. Those knowable only through experience are not demonstrable, while those knowable without experience are.
claims: Connotative properties knowable only by experience are not demonstrable.
Connotative properties knowable without experience are demonstrable.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e472.summary: Examples for the third conclusion: that heat is calefactive or that the sun can produce a worm is known only by experience; that every triangle has three angles equal to two right angles, or that composite substance is corruptible, is known without it.
claims: 'Heat is calefactive' is known only by experience.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e483.summary: A technical note on syllogistic form. When such demonstrations proceed from simply first premises, the premises must be taken in oblique, not direct, form ('whatever has an intellective soul in it is susceptible of learning'). If the abstract served as middle, a premise would be false ('every man is an intellective soul'). If the concrete served as middle, a premise would not be simply first. The oblique premise is not itself simply first, but it includes per se as a part the simply first proposition. So for demonstration from simply first propositions one premise must be hypothetical ('if the soul is in something, it is susceptible of learning').
claims: Demonstrations of properties of wholes through parts require premises in oblique form.
Using the abstract as middle term makes a premise false.
Using the concrete as middle term makes a premise not simply first.
Demonstration from simply first propositions requires a hypothetical premise containing the first proposition.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e557.summary: Fourth conclusion: every negative property whose opposite can be evidently known to be predicated of something as its first subject can be demonstrated, through that first subject as middle, in a second-figure syllogism ('whatever has three angles equal to two right angles is a triangle; no quadrangle is a triangle; so no quadrangle has three...'). For other cases no certain rule is easy to give. Such conclusions are often demonstrated through definitions expressing parts, above all in mathematics.
claims: A negative property whose opposite is evidently known of a first subject is demonstrable in the second figure.
There is no easy general rule for the demonstrability of other negative properties.
In mathematics, conclusions are often demonstrated through definitions expressing parts.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e592.summary: States the answer: not every property is demonstrable a priori of its first subject.
claims: Not every property is demonstrable a priori of its first subject.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e606.summary: First objection from Aristotle (Posterior Analytics I, on the universal): a universal is what is demonstrated of every instance and of the first subject, so a universal is always demonstrated of its first subject.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e617.summary: Second objection from the same chapter: when it is shown that the first subject has two right angles, the demonstration is universal and per se of that subject, and only in a way not per se of others. So the universal is always demonstrable per se of its first subject and secondarily of others.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e633.summary: Third objection: according to chapters 9 and 7, every demonstrative science concerns genus, axioms and per se properties, so properties are considered in demonstrative science.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e644.summary: Fourth objection: Aristotle constantly gives examples of such properties, like eclipse and thunder.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e649.summary: Fifth objection: in Posterior Analytics II Aristotle teaches demonstration through every kind of cause, so whatever has a cause of its inherence in a subject is demonstrable through that cause, and these properties have such causes.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e660.summary: Sixth objection: according to Posterior Analytics II, those who know the 'that' seek the 'why', and the question 'why', like the others, seeks a middle term.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e670.summary: Answers the first objection: Aristotle speaks of a universal that belongs first to a subject, whether or not it is demonstrable. When it is demonstrable, it is first demonstrated of its first subject, the one it is predicated of adequately (of all and only that subject), and of others secondarily.
claims: Aristotle's 'universal' belongs first to a subject whether or not it is demonstrable.
When demonstrable, a universal is first demonstrated of its adequate subject.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e688.summary: Applies the same answer to the whole chapter of Aristotle cited, which answers the second objection.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e693.summary: Answers the third objection: Aristotle takes 'demonstrative science' strictly for demonstration, and demonstration employs properties whether or not they are demonstrable, since they can serve as principles or in some way as middles.
claims: Properties enter demonstration as principles or middles even when not themselves demonstrable.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e706.summary: Adds that 'demonstration is of properties' does not entail 'of all properties'. In every science some properties are demonstrable and some not.
claims: In every science some properties are demonstrable and some are not.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e713.summary: Answers the fifth objection: demonstration through every kind of cause is particular, not universal.
claims: Demonstration through every kind of cause is particular, not universal.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e720.summary: Explains 'particular demonstration'. In one sense it is a demonstration not of the first subject, as in Posterior Analytics I. In another it is a demonstration whose conclusion is not universal, either as to supposita or as to time: not concluding the predicate of every instance, or not of all times but of a determinate time. Such demonstrations from simply necessary propositions are usually hypothetical, conditional or temporal. For example, 'the moon is eclipsable' is known only by experience, but once it is known one can demonstrate that at a given time the moon will be eclipsed, through the interposition of the earth.
claims: Demonstration can be particular as to subject, supposita or time.
Demonstrations from simply necessary premises concerning extrinsic causes are usually hypothetical, conditional or temporal.
'The moon is eclipsable' is known only by experience.
Eclipses at determinate times are demonstrable through the earth's interposition.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e780.summary: Such demonstration uses an extrinsic cause, and Aristotle's examples are all particular, involving present, past and future tenses. The reason is that an extrinsic cause causes the thing's actual existence, so it cannot serve as a middle without some temporal determination. Otherwise everything could be demonstrated through God, the extrinsic efficient and final cause of all, which is unfitting. So by universal, a priori demonstration no such property is demonstrable of its first subject.
claims: Demonstration through extrinsic causes always involves temporal determination.
If extrinsic causes yielded universal demonstrations, everything could be demonstrated through God.
No such property is demonstrable of its first subject by universal a priori demonstration.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e811.summary: A qualification: if a property imports an inhering absolute thing and also connotes a determinate cause, even though the thing could be caused by various causes, it can be demonstrated of its first subject. If the moon could be illuminated by the sun or another planet, 'the moon is illuminable' is indemonstrable and known only by experience. But a name signifying the moon's illumination and connoting the sun specifically could be demonstrated: once experience shows that the sun is luminous, and that it can be directly opposed to the moon at a time when no other planet is, it follows demonstratively, even if never observed, that the moon is illuminable by the sun.
claims: A property connoting a determinate cause can be demonstrated of its first subject.
'The moon is illuminable' is indemonstrable if several causes could illuminate it.
'The moon is illuminable by the sun' can be demonstrated from experientially known premises.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e857.summary: Answers the sixth objection: those who know the 'that' particularly, not universally, seek the 'why' and so seek the middle of a particular demonstration. Aristotle's examples ('we know that the moon is eclipsed, we ask why') concern the existence of things.
claims: The search for the 'why' concerns the middle of a particular demonstration.
Aristotle's examples concern questions of existence.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e875.summary: Raises an objection: scientific knowledge does not concern existing things except contingently, since being in act is accidental to them. All these temporal propositions are contingent and so do not belong to demonstration.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e884.summary: Replies: the subject of a science need not exist in act, but in many or all cases it must be able to, and on Aristotle's view must sometimes be posited in act. So the conclusion is not 'the moon is eclipsed' but 'the moon is eclipsed when so opposed to the sun'. That is necessary according to Aristotle, though not in truth given God's absolute power, and on his view it is demonstrable. Grosseteste says the same: necessary hypothetical (conditional or temporal) propositions are formed from frequently occurring contingents.
claims: The subject of a science need not exist in act but must be able to.
Necessary conditional or temporal propositions can be formed from contingent events.
Such propositions are necessary per Aristotle but not absolutely, given God's absolute power.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e919.summary: This also answers the second part of the objection: by 'contingent propositions' Aristotle means necessary propositions formed from the same terms.
claims: Aristotle's 'contingent propositions' in demonstration are necessary propositions formed from contingent terms.

wo8uy7-d1e105-d1e927.summary: Answers the principal argument: there is a reason why one property is demonstrable and another not. Some properties presuppose that the subject has really distinct parts without which they could not belong to it. Through distinct knowledge of those parts one reaches knowledge of the property, so these are demonstrable through a definition expressing the parts. Others presuppose no distinction of parts and remain when any part is removed, so nothing intrinsic to the subject belongs to them prior to or more evidently than the subject, and they are indemonstrable. The paragraph ends by announcing a further question annexed to the second.
claims: Properties presupposing really distinct parts are demonstrable through definitions expressing those parts.
Properties presupposing no distinction of parts are indemonstrable.

wo8uy7-d1e105.summary: Prologue question 4, the second incidental question, asks whether every property is demonstrable a priori of its first subject. Ockham classifies properties as absolute-inherent, motion-importing, connotative, and negative. He argues that properties importing a formally inhering absolute thing are never demonstrable of their first subject, for three reasons: such propositions are immediate; no definition expressing determinate parts can serve as middle, since the subject is as simple as the accident; and their first knowledge comes only through experience of singulars. They can be demonstrated of non-first subjects through the first subject, with careful attention to oblique and hypothetical premise forms. Connotative properties are demonstrable when knowable without experience, and negative ones when the opposite is known of a first subject (second figure). Answering Aristotelian objections, he argues that demonstrations through extrinsic causes such as eclipses are particular and temporal or hypothetical, never universal a priori. Their necessity is relative to Aristotle's assumptions, not to God's absolute power. Properties connoting a determinate cause can still be demonstrated. What makes a property demonstrable is that it presupposes really distinct parts of its subject.
claims: Not every property is demonstrable a priori of its first subject.
Absolute inherent properties are known of their first subject only through experience.
Demonstrability depends on the property presupposing really distinct parts of the subject.
Demonstrations through extrinsic causes are particular and temporal or hypothetical.
The necessity of such hypothetical propositions holds per Aristotle but not absolutely, given God's power.
